Glutton
glut'n
n. (one who eats to excess; in the law, a capital charge against a rebellious son, and in the Gospels a slander against the Son of man)
From Latin gluto, a glutton, from glutire, to swallow, through Old French gluton. The Hebrew at Deuteronomy 21:20 is zolel, a squanderer or riotous eater; the Greek slander at Matthew 11:19 is phagos, an eater.

Biblical Definition

Gluttony appears in the law not as a private failing but as evidence in a capital case. The parents of the stubborn son bring their charge to the elders: “This our son is stubborn and rebellious, he will not obey our voice; he is a glutton, and a drunkard” (Deuteronomy 21:20). The two vices are named together because both are the visible fruit of a will that has thrown off authority; the sin prosecuted is the rebellion, and the appetite is the proof of it. Proverbs keeps the pairing and adds the outcome: “For the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty: and drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags” (Proverbs 23:21), following the warning not to sit among “riotous eaters of flesh” (Proverbs 23:20). Then the word is turned into a slander against our Lord. “The Son of man came eating and drinking, and they say, Behold a man gluttonous, and a winebibber, a friend of publicans and sinners” (Matthew 11:19). John came neither eating nor drinking and was called demon-possessed; Christ came eating and drinking and was called a glutton. The generation was not evaluating conduct at all — it was refusing both messengers — and our Lord's answer is that wisdom is justified of her children.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a glutton as one who indulges to excess in eating, and figuratively one greedy of anything to excess.

expand to see more

GLUTTON, n. One who indulges to excess in eating.

2. One eager of any thing to excess.

GLUTTONY, n. Excess in eating; extravagant indulgence of the appetite for food.

Their sumptuous gluttonies and gorgeous feasts.

APPETITE, n. The desire of food or drink; a painful sensation occasioned by hunger or thirst.

Key Scripture

Deuteronomy 21:20 — "And they shall say unto the elders of his city, This our son is stubborn and rebellious, he will not obey our voice; he is a glutton, and a drunkard."

Proverbs 23:21 — "For the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty: and drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags."

Proverbs 23:20 — "Be not among winebibbers; among riotous eaters of flesh:"

Matthew 11:19 — "The Son of man came eating and drinking, and they say, Behold a man gluttonous, and a winebibber, a friend of publicans and sinners. But wisdom is justified of her children."

Modern Corruption

Gluttony is the one deadly sin the modern church has stopped naming, having outsourced the whole subject to dietetics and body image.

expand to see more

Of the traditional catalogue of grave sins, gluttony is the one now almost never preached. Two pressures produced the silence. The first is that the subject has been transferred wholesale to medicine and diet culture, where the categories are health, metabolism, and appearance rather than sin, appetite, and self-government — so a pastor who raises it sounds as though he is commenting on his people's bodies. The second is that gluttony is the respectable indulgence of respectable congregations, and men do not readily preach against what they are doing. Scripture keeps it in the list, pairs it with drunkenness every time, and treats both as marks of a will that will not be governed.

The correction must run in both directions. Naming gluttony is not licence to make the body itself the measure of holiness; that is its own ancient error, and the apostle warns against a will-worship of neglecting the body that has no honour in satisfying the flesh. The biblical category is appetite ungoverned, which can be as true of a thin man as a heavy one. Deuteronomy 21:20 is the key: the charge is rebellion, and the eating is evidence. And Matthew 11:19 stands as a permanent guard against the opposite excess, since our Lord Himself — who fasted forty days and also came eating and drinking — was called a glutton by men who simply would not receive Him.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew zolel, a riotous eater or squanderer — Deuteronomy 21:20, Proverbs 23:21; Greek phagos, an eater — Matthew 11:19; Latin glutire, to swallow.

expand to see more

Hebrew zolel — one who is vile, a squanderer, a riotous eater; Deuteronomy 21:20 and Proverbs 23:21.

Hebrew soba — drunkard, the constant companion term in both texts.

Greek phagos — an eater, a glutton; Matthew 11:19 and Luke 7:34, both in the mouths of accusers.

Greek gaster — the belly; Titus 1:12, “slow bellies,” and Philippians 3:19, “whose God is their belly.”

Latin gluto, from glutire, to swallow — the source of the English word.

Usage

"“He is a glutton, and a drunkard” — the appetites cited as evidence of rebellion."

"“Drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags” — the poverty that follows the table."

"“Behold a man gluttonous” — a slander against Christ, and the proof they would receive no messenger."
